A class of 200 students takes a difficult exam. The 10 students with the very highest scores are given a 'genius' award and asked to retake an equally hard exam the next day. On average, compared to their first score, their second score will most likely be:
choices: About the same, since ability doesn't change overnight
Higher, since they've proven they're the most skilled students
Lower, because the award causes overconfidence and worse performance
Lower, because extreme scores are partly due to luck, and regression to the mean pulls the average back down

questions.q: You will interview 100 candidates one at a time in random order and must accept or reject each immediately; a rejected candidate can't be recalled, and you win only by accepting the single best candidate overall. Under the optimal 'look-then-leap' strategy — reject the first ~37 candidates outright, then accept the next one who beats all of those — what is the approximate probability of picking the single best candidate?

Participants spin a wheel rigged to land on either 10 or 65, then are asked to estimate what percentage of UN countries are in Africa. Those who saw 10 guessed lower on average than those who saw 65 — even though the wheel's result was obviously random and irrelevant. What cognitive bias does this famous Tversky & Kahneman experiment demonstrate?

A study compares two kidney-stone treatments. Treatment A cures 81 of 87 small stones (93%) and 192 of 263 large stones (73%). Treatment B cures 234 of 270 small stones (87%) and 55 of 80 large stones (69%). Treatment A has the higher cure rate for small stones AND for large stones — yet combining all 350 patients per treatment, Treatment B has the higher overall cure rate. What explains this?
choices: The overall totals are lower-quality data and should be ignored in favor of the subgroup rates
It's impossible unless the two treatments were tested on completely different patient populations
One of the four percentages must be miscalculated, since this is a contradiction
Simpson's paradox — Treatment A was used on far more of the harder large-stone cases, which pulls its combined average down

questions.q: Software teams estimate a project will take 3 months. Historically, similar past estimates by the same teams for similar projects have taken on average 2.5x longer than estimated — a pattern they are fully aware of. What is the well-documented cognitive bias where people systematically underestimate task duration even while knowing past tasks ran over?
A standard 8×8 chessboard has its two opposite corner squares (both the same colour) removed. Using dominoes that each cover exactly two adjacent squares, can the remaining 62 squares be fully tiled?
choices: Only if the removed squares are adjacent
Only if an odd number of dominoes is used
